title: LEGO.com brings back Darksaber, Spider-Man and Straw Topper gifts with purchase

title: Vanished LEGO Ideas Supernatural project mysteriously reappears
summary: A LEGO Ideas 10K submission that disappeared without explanation has quietly returned to the platform, rejoining 49 other projects awaiting official review.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
A fan-made LEGO Ideas submission called Dean's Baby – Supernatural (TV Show), which recreates the 1967 Chevrolet Impala from the TV series in 450 pieces, vanished from the LEGO Ideas site over a week ago after hitting the 10,000-vote threshold needed to enter LEGO's official review stage. No reason was given for its removal at the time.

According to Brick Fanatics, the project has now reappeared on the platform with no official explanation from the LEGO Group about why it disappeared or why it's back. Its return brings the current 10K review batch back up to 50 submissions, and the project will now go through the same review process as the others, with an equal chance of becoming an official LEGO set.

This isn't the first time this has happened — Brick Fanatics notes that other qualifying projects, including The NeverEnding Story, Gothic Castle, and The Hearthian's Ship from Outer Wilds, were similarly pulled from consideration back in 2023 after reaching 10K support.

## Why it matters
LEGO Ideas is one of the few routes for fan concepts to become official sets, so any unexplained removal (and reinstatement) understandably worries builders who've put time and votes into supporting a project. For fans of Supernatural, the Impala's return means there's once again a chance — however slim — of an official set down the line.

## What to watch next
It's worth watching whether the LEGO Group ever issues an official statement clarifying why the project was removed and restored, and how it fares alongside the other 49 submissions in this review round.

title: LEGO Donkey Kong Arcade set gets stamp of approval from Shigeru Miyamoto
summary: Set designer Carl Merriam says Nintendo's Shigeru Miyamoto is 'very happy' with 72051 Donkey Kong Arcade, revealing the engineering headaches behind its barrel-rolling mechanism.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
Designer Carl Merriam, who worked on 72051 Donkey Kong Arcade alongside sets like 71411 The Mighty Bowser and 10497 Galaxy Explorer, has spoken to The Verge about building LEGO's recreation of the classic 1981 arcade cabinet.

Merriam says he hasn't met Donkey Kong and Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto directly, but understands Miyamoto is 'very happy' with how the set turned out. According to Brick Fanatics, Nintendo did have one request during development, though the exact detail of that request wasn't specified in the available reporting.

The set faithfully recreates the arcade cabinet using the mass-produced blue housing rather than the rarer red version from the original run. Its standout feature is a working barrel mechanism: Jumpman (better known as Mario) can dodge barrels rolling down the pink scaffolding, though he can't climb between levels.

Merriam revealed that controlling the barrels' speed was the toughest challenge, saying he 'rolled thousands of barrels down those tracks' during development. The team also tried various ways of returning barrels to the top, including gears and levers, before settling on a simpler solution — just using more barrels. The finished chute holds 14 barrels with room for up to 20, creating what Merriam calls an 'infinite barrel loop'.

## Why it matters
Designer insight like this gives builders a rare look at how LEGO translates classic gaming mechanics into physical, playable models. For fans of the Donkey Kong set or retro gaming crossovers, Miyamoto's approval adds a layer of authenticity and could boost interest in the set among both LEGO collectors and Nintendo fans.

## What to watch next
It's worth watching for further details on what Nintendo's specific request was, as this wasn't fully explained in current reporting — a detail collectors may want clarified before drawing conclusions about Nintendo's creative input on the set.

title: LEGO's Donkey Kong Arcade set shown in action at SDCC
summary: LEGO's new 72051 Donkey Kong Arcade set has been officially unveiled and demoed at San Diego Comic-Con, with barrel-dodging action captured on video ahead of its August launch.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
LEGO has officially revealed the 72051 Donkey Kong Arcade set, showing it in action on the show floor at San Diego Comic-Con. Footage from Beyond the Brick shows the mechanism at work: pressing a button on the cabinet sends a barrel rolling down pink scaffolding, while a joystick moves Jumpman (the character who'd later become Mario) side to side and up and down to hop over it.

The set has 1,367 pieces and is priced at £149.99 / $199.99 / €169.99, making it smaller and cheaper than the retiring 10323 PAC-MAN Arcade. It's not a fully playable recreation — Jumpman's movement is limited and can't travel the full height of the cabinet, and the barrels actually run on a separate track behind him rather than being avoidable in any real sense. So it's more about recreating the look of the classic arcade gameplay than offering genuine challenge, sitting somewhere between the simulated action of PAC-MAN Arcade and the more skill-based 11374 Arcade Pinball Machine.

72051 Donkey Kong Arcade is up for pre-order now in some regions, with a full launch set for 1 August.

## Why it matters
Arcade-style LEGO sets have proven popular with collectors and display builders, and this continues the trend of officially licensed Nintendo sets following on from Super Mario and PAC-MAN. For fans of the format, it's a smaller, more affordable entry point than PAC-MAN Arcade, and the limited but tactile play mechanism could appeal to both collectors and anyone into modding or custom brick tinkering.

## What to watch next
It'll be worth watching whether the custom building community attempts to mod the set for fuller playability, potentially trading off stability or looks for more authentic gameplay. Full hands-on reviews are also expected closer to the August launch.

It was Graphic Designer Melody Flores, drawing on her own experience with Day of the Dead traditions, who made the case for leaving the skull plain. Her point: La Catrina is fundamentally a skull figure — the Lady of Death — and doesn't need extra decoration to be recognisable or authentic.

Instead, the team put decorative effort into skull patterns printed on La Catrina's dress, giving the model detail elsewhere while keeping the skull itself true to how the character is traditionally depicted.

It's a good reminder that design choices on LEGO sets aren't always about budget — sometimes they're deliberate calls rooted in getting cultural representation right. title: LEGO Botanicals meets pop culture in Olivia Rodrigo Flower Bouquet set
summary: Brickset has reviewed 11507 Olivia Rodrigo's Flower Bouquet, a 400-piece set that's part of the new Editions line but also carries the Botanicals label — reportedly the first licensed Botanicals set.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
Brickset has published a review of 11507 Olivia Rodrigo's Flower Bouquet, one of five newly announced Editions sets themed around the singer Olivia Rodrigo. Unusually, this particular set is also classified under LEGO's Botanicals theme, blending two distinct lines on one box. It comes in at 400 pieces — not the smallest set in the Olivia Rodrigo lineup, but the flower subject matter makes it feel more compact.

According to Brickset, the box artwork gives prominence to both the Editions and Botanicals branding, though the overall look leans towards the white Editions aesthetic rather than Botanicals' usual darker packaging style. Brickset notes this appears to be the first Botanicals set built around a licensed property, marking a notable first for the theme.

## Why it matters
Botanicals sets have built a loyal following among adult builders and display fans for their realistic flower and plant designs. Seeing the theme cross over into licensed territory — alongside a chart-topping music artist, no less — signals LEGO may be testing whether Botanicals' appeal can extend beyond generic nature-inspired sets. For collectors, it's a set that ticks two boxes at once: fans of the artist and fans of botanical builds.

## What to watch next
It's worth watching whether other Editions or licensed themes get similar Botanicals crossover treatment in future, and how well this hybrid set is received by both music fans and plant-set collectors.
